model: claude-opus-5-5 in a Claude Code session
system: You are a careful experimenter who designs measurements. You can only use the tools you are given, and only a limited number of measurements. Choose each measurement so that it helps to tell the two models apart, and say why. At the end say which model the measurements favour and how sure you are, or say that they do not tell the models apart. Do not say that a model is true because it fits.
task: A block of 2 kg slides on a table and slows down; the launcher of this rig cannot start it faster than 4 m/s. Two models of the drag compete: linear drag, v = v0 exp(-g t), and quadratic drag, v = v0 / (1 + k v0 t), with g and k unknown. Each reading of the speed has a standard uncertainty of 0.1 m/s. Choose at most 8 measurements, with a start speed of at most 4 m/s, that tell the two models apart.

steps.text: Plan: the two models differ in how the decay depends on the start speed. Linear drag gives v/v0 = exp(-g t), the same fractional decay for every v0; quadratic drag decays faster at high v0 (rate k v0). So I compare a high start speed (4 m/s, the maximum, where the quadratic effect is strongest) with a low one (1 m/s) at the same times. First I measure at v0 = 4 m/s at t = 1 s and t = 4 s to learn the time scale, and v0 = 1 m/s at the same two times.

Results so far: at v0 = 4, v(1) = 3.50 and v(4) = 2.23; at v0 = 1, v(1) = 1.12 and v(4) = 0.91. A linear model fitted to the 4 m/s runs (g about 0.14 /s) predicts v(4) about 0.57 for v0 = 1, 3.4 sigma below the reading 0.91; the slow run decays much less in fraction than the fast one, which points to a start-speed-dependent rate, as quadratic drag has. But a quadratic fit to v0 = 4 (k about 0.045) is itself somewhat strained (it predicts v(1) about 3.39 vs 3.50). The largest difference between the models is at long times, where exponential and hyperbolic tails part: with these fits, linear predicts v(10) about 0.25 (v0=1) and 0.99 (v0=4); quadratic predicts about 0.69 and 1.43. So I measure at t = 10 s for both start speeds.

At t = 10 s: v0 = 1 gives 0.68 (quadratic about 0.69, linear about 0.25) and v0 = 4 gives 1.25. A single quadratic k about 0.048 /m fits all six readings with chi-square about 7 for 5 degrees of freedom; the best single linear g (about 0.1 /s) gives chi-square about 47, because the fractional decay depends strongly on start speed. Two readings remain. I use them as an out-of-sample check, not for fitting: an intermediate start speed v0 = 2 at t = 10 s, where quadratic with k = 0.048 predicts 2/(1+0.96) = 1.02, and a linear model fitted to the slow runs (g about 0.04) would predict about 1.34 while one fitted to the fast runs (g about 0.13) would predict about 0.55. And a repeat of v0 = 1 at t = 1 s, the reading furthest from the quadratic fit (1.12 vs 0.95), to see whether it was noise.

Conclusion. Eight readings (v0, t -> v): (4,1) 3.50; (4,4) 2.23; (4,10) 1.25; (1,1) 1.12 and 1.06; (1,4) 0.91; (1,10) 0.68; (2,10) 0.98. The decisive feature is that the fractional decay depends on the start speed: after 10 s the 1 m/s block keeps 68 % of its speed, the 2 m/s block 49 %, the 4 m/s block 31 %. Linear drag predicts the same fraction for every start speed, so no single g fits: the best compromise leaves several readings 2 to 7 sigma off (chi-square roughly 50 for 7 degrees of freedom). Quadratic drag with k about 0.048 per metre fits every reading within about 1.7 sigma (chi-square roughly 9 for 7 degrees of freedom), and it predicted the held-out v0 = 2, t = 10 s reading (1.02 predicted, 0.98 measured) before it was taken. The measurements therefore clearly favour quadratic drag over linear drag; I am confident in that comparison (a likelihood ratio of order exp(20)). This does not show that quadratic drag is the true law: it is only the better of the two candidates on these data. One mild tension remains: both readings at v0 = 1, t = 1 s lie above the start speed (mean 1.09 +/- 0.07), which no slowing model can produce; at about 1.3 to 2 sigma it is consistent with noise, but a mixed law (for example linear plus quadratic, or added friction) was not tested and cannot be excluded with 8 readings.
